\chapter{Too Dear: The Answer and the Counter}
\label{ch:mw-bargain}
\hlchaptermodality{28}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something is very expensive and ask for it a little cheaper, completing a three-turn bargaining exchange without learning a single new Devanagari sign.}

A strengthener, a softener, and a second asking word each arrive by ear before their spelling, join two source-printed lines, and close as a three-turn exchange scored separately in listening, speaking, reading, and writing.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ghaṇo]{Hear \emph{ghaṇo} — very}

\label{lesson:MW-C23-hear-ghano}



\begin{quote}
Recall the price payoff, the request payoff, and the six-word weather payoff, then say expensive and cheap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{ghaṇo} — \textbf{very}
\end{quote}

Two beats. The first carries the breathed \emph{gh} of \emph{ghar}; the second carries the same retroflex \emph{ṇ} as \emph{kitṇo} and \emph{pāṇī}.

The source prints it in front of a description, where English puts \emph{very}: the food is \emph{ghaṇo} tasty. Put it in front of \emph{mahaṅgo} and you have said more than that a thing costs money: you have said it costs too much, which is the whole reason a bargain begins.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-6-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 6}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ghaṇo]{\mw{घणो} — very, on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C23-ghano}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{very}, then write home and clarified butter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{घ}} + \textbf{\mw{णो}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{घणो}} — \emph{ghaṇo} — very
\end{quote}

Three signs, none of them new. Write \textbf{\mw{घर}}, \textbf{\mw{घी}}, and \textbf{\mw{घणो}} one under the other: the same \textbf{\mw{घ}} opens all three. Then write \textbf{\mw{कितणो}} beside \textbf{\mw{घणो}} and check the \textbf{\mw{णो}} at the end is drawn the same way in both.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\mw{घणो}}, cover it, wait five seconds, and write it from the sound.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-6-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 6}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ye ghaṇo mahaṅgo hai]{Hear \emph{ye ghaṇo mahaṅgo hai} — this is very expensive}

\label{lesson:MW-C23-hear-price-answer}



\begin{quote}
Say the price question, write \emph{very} and expensive, then say and write the sweet crumbled wheat dessert.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{ye ghaṇo mahaṅgo hai} — \textbf{this is very expensive}
\end{quote}

Four words, every one of them already yours. \emph{ye} points, \emph{ghaṇo} strengthens, \emph{mahaṅgo} describes, \emph{hai} closes. The order is fixed: the strengthener always comes before the word it strengthens.

Say it once flat, as a fact, and once slowly, the way you would actually say it across a counter when you mean to keep talking. The words do not change; the pace does, and the pace is what tells a seller a bargain has begun.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}; \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-6-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 6}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ye ghaṇo mahaṅgo hai.]{\mw{ये} \mw{घणो} \mw{महंगो} \mw{है।} — the reply on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C23-price-answer}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this is very expensive}, write temple, then write \textbf{\mw{ख}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{ये} | \mw{घणो} | \mw{महंगो} | \mw{है।}}
\end{quote}

Four written words, each written before. The dot above \textbf{\mw{महंगो}} is the same \textbf{\mw{ं}} that sits in \textbf{\mw{मंदिर}}; it is the only mark in the line that is easy to drop, so check for it last.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read the line once. Cover it for ten seconds and write all four words. Open the model, check the dot first, and repair only the word that changed.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}; \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-6-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 6}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\label{lesson:MW-R23-answer-two}



\begin{quote}
Recall the seven-word food payoff, write \textbf{\mw{य}}, write lentils, then write the total question from the last chapter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Hear the two lines in the wrong order and say which one has to come first. Give both meanings. Read two cards. Write both from sound, one under the other, and read the pair aloud as a single exchange.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[thoṛu]{Hear \emph{thoṛu} — a little}

\label{lesson:MW-C23-hear-thodu}



\begin{quote}
Recall the three-word transport payoff, then say cart and bus and write both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{thoṛu} — \textbf{a little}
\end{quote}

Two beats. The first is the breathed \emph{th} of \emph{ṭhelā}; the middle carries the flapped \emph{ṛ} you already say inside \emph{kapṛā} and \emph{ghoṛo}.

Hold it against \emph{ghaṇo}, which you learned four lessons ago. \emph{ghaṇo} makes a word bigger; \emph{thoṛu} makes an amount smaller. A seller hears the difference at once, and it is the difference between complaining about a price and offering to meet it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[thoṛu]{\mw{थोड़ु} — a little, on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C23-thodu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a little}, then write clothes and horse.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{थो}} + \textbf{\mw{ड़ु}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{थोड़ु}} — \emph{thoṛu} — a little
\end{quote}

Three of this track's most easily confused marks meet in four signs. \textbf{\mw{ड़}} is \textbf{\mw{ड}} with the nukta under it, exactly as in \textbf{\mw{कपड़ा}} and \textbf{\mw{घोड़ो}}; the short \textbf{\mw{ु}} hangs beneath it. Write \textbf{\mw{कपड़ा}}, \textbf{\mw{घोड़ो}}, and \textbf{\mw{थोड़ु}} in a column and check that all three dots sit at the same height.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\mw{थोड़ु}}, cover it, wait five seconds, and write it. Check the dot, then the \textbf{\mw{ु}} below it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[karo]{Hear \emph{karo} — make it}

\label{lesson:MW-C23-hear-karo}



\begin{quote}
Recall the seven-word shopping payoff, then write \emph{a little} and cheap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{karo} — \textbf{make it; do it}
\end{quote}

Two beats, and the ending is one you have already heard. Say \emph{dikhāvo} and \emph{karo} one after the other: both close on the same \emph{-o}, because both are the same kind of asking word, said to one person across a counter.

\emph{dikhāvo} asks somebody to show you a thing. \emph{karo} asks them to make something so — and what they are to make it, you say in front of the word.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[karo]{\mw{करो} — make it, on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C23-karo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{make it}, write \textbf{\mw{राम}}, write \textbf{\mw{ख}}, then write \emph{how much} and \emph{very}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{क}} + \textbf{\mw{रो}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{करो}} — \emph{karo} — make it
\end{quote}

Three signs, and the middle one is \textbf{\mw{र}}, the very first sign this book taught. Set \textbf{\mw{करो}} beside \textbf{\mw{ख}} and say both: \textbf{\mw{क}} and \textbf{\mw{ख}} differ only by breath, and only one of them belongs in this word.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\mw{करो}}, cover it, wait five seconds, and write it from the sound. Check that you wrote \textbf{\mw{क}} and not \textbf{\mw{ख}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[thoṛu sasto karo]{Hear \emph{thoṛu sasto karo} — make it a little cheaper}

\label{lesson:MW-C23-hear-bargain-request}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this is very expensive}, then say item and cheap and write both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{thoṛu sasto karo} — \textbf{make it a little cheaper}
\end{quote}

Three words, all yours: \emph{thoṛu} shrinks the amount, \emph{sasto} is the \emph{sastā} you learned in Chapter 19, and \emph{karo} asks.

The source prints \emph{sasto} here, with \emph{-o} rather than the \emph{-ā} the earlier lesson taught. Both forms are used; the ending shifts with what the word is describing. Learn the printed line as it stands, and treat \emph{sastā} and \emph{sasto} as the same word wearing two endings rather than two different words.

Say the whole exchange in order: ask the price, say it is too much, then this.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[thoṛu sasto karo.]{\mw{थोड़ु} \mw{सस्तो} \mw{करो।} — the counter-offer on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C23-bargain-request}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\mw{्}} on its own, then write wife and item, and point to the vowel-killer in each.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{थोड़ु} | \mw{सस्तो} | \mw{करो।}}
\end{quote}

Three written words. \textbf{\mw{सस्तो}} is the \textbf{\mw{सस्ता}} of Chapter 19 with \textbf{\mw{ो}} where \textbf{\mw{ा}} stood; its vowel-killer between the two \textbf{\mw{स}} does not move. The stop at the end is the \textbf{\mw{।}} you have written since Chapter 9.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read the line once. Cover it for ten seconds and write all three words. Open the model and check two marks first: the dot under \textbf{\mw{ड़}} and the vowel-killer inside \textbf{\mw{सस्तो}}. Repair only the word that changed.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Retrieve \emph{a little} and \emph{make it}}

\label{lesson:MW-R23-bargain-two}



\begin{quote}
Recall the five-word transport payoff, then write vehicle and \emph{very}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Hear each word alone, out of its line, and give its meaning. Read two cards. Write both from sound. Then rebuild the whole counter-offer from those two words plus the one you already had, and say it once at speaking pace.

\section[Practice]{Payoff — ask, react, counter}

\label{lesson:MW-C23-counter-four}



\begin{quote}
Recall the price payoff and the seven-word shopping payoff, then write clothes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Three turns, in this order and no other.

1. Hear the three lines shuffled and put them back in order. 2. Produce all three from meaning cues, as one continuous exchange. 3. Read the three printed lines and say who speaks which. 4. Write all three from dictation, without a model.

Pass each skill separately. You can now open a price, react to it, and make one counter-offer. Hearing a number in reply, agreeing a final price, and paying are still untaught.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}; \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-6-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 6}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Close the writing loop for \mw{़}, \mw{्} and \mw{ं}}

\label{lesson:MW-R23-script-close}



\begin{quote}
Recall the three-turn bargaining payoff, say expensive, then write \textbf{\mw{ख}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Three marks change a word without adding a letter, and all three are easy to lose. Write each on its own from a spoken cue: the dot under a letter, the vowel-killer, the dot above the headstroke.

Then write \textbf{\mw{थोड़ु}}, \textbf{\mw{कपड़ा}}, \textbf{\mw{पत्नी}}, \textbf{\mw{बच्चा}}, and \textbf{\mw{महंगो}} from dictation and mark which of the three you used in each. Finish with both lines of this chapter. Repair only the missed mark and rewrite its word once.
